title: The Jesuit Who Remembered Backwards

lines.text: A Jesuit read random characters once, then said them backwards.
Scholars called his memory a miracle. The truth was much older.
In 1595, Matteo Ricci settled in Nanchang, in Ming China.
lines.say: In fifteen ninety-five, Mat-tay-oh Ree-chee settled in Nan-chahng, in Ming China.

lines.text: The governor of Jiangxi asked him to teach his art to his three sons.
lines.say: The governor of Jyahng-shee asked him to teach his art to his three sons.

lines.text: It looked like a gift. It was a technique he had learned in Rome.
Cicero tells how it began. The poet Simonides, the story goes, was called outside from a banquet.
lines.say: Cicero tells how it began. The poet Sy-mon-ih-deez, the story goes, was called outside from a banquet.

lines.text: Moments later the roof fell in, crushing the guests.
He identified the bodies by remembering where each guest had reclined.
This is the method of loci, from the Latin for places.
lines.say: This is the method of loh-sye, from the Latin for places.

lines.text: Picture a building you know well. Leave one vivid image in each room.
Then walk through it in your mind. The order of the rooms keeps the order of the things.
Ricci hoped the scholars would grow curious about his God. It did not work out that way.

caption: In 1595 the scholars of Nanchang thought Matteo Ricci had a miraculous memory. He was using the method of loci, the memory palace trick, and it can be learned. A true story, fact-checked. Tomorrow: Art & Music. Curiouser No. 13
